course: Because of the disaster, the course had to be turned into a 50% midterm - 50% final one. Otherwise, it would have also included presentations (that included covering up the political philosophers by reading their books and talking about their thought provocation methods). Therefore on a term where you are extremely busy, this detailed presentation may be too much to handle (like a 7 course schedule busy). The general course material is heavy in nature anyway, so, take this course if you are really sure you are interested in political philosophy and/or can spend hours on talking/researching about it. Knowing as much of the most prominent political philosophers is a big plus to increase confidence and familiarity with the material.

instructor: One of the best teachers in the department. He is always positive and puts a lot of effort into explaining things to his students. Even after the lesson is over, he continues to talk because he loves to teach. He is a real teacher.
He is so understanding and kind to his students. Also, he explained what he expected from us for the midterm and final exams. This is rare, thank you.

The good points: He takes a critical approach to texts and IPE, rather than showing PowerPoint in lectures and informatively showing what we would normally read (almost no one reads). Especially Mr. Akrivoulis' critiques of the liberal point of view and the approaches he presented to the IPE were really stimulating. Perhaps the way he teaches courses and the approaches he brings to the subjects make him the most valuable instructor of Bilkent IR. Yes, I think his participation in the course is low, but this is because the course is mostly irrelevant to what he asks in the exam. Students find it unnecessary to come to class (since they do not do the regular readings, they expect from the instructor to teach the topics) because the teacher does not tell anything directly about the exam. In other words, those who come to the class actually like his style, but even though many people criticize his style, he should never deviate from this path. There are few people who like his style a lot. I think he can dive into the depth of the topics directly and without repetition. I also appreciate his openness. In his own words, he can boldly explain the topics "hidden under the carpet". One of the features that makes him special is that he does not stick to "safe" topics. Thank you.

The downsides: He has problems with timing. He comes to class late and finishes late (although I like that, I wouldn't like it if I had another class after this class). Also, since most people in the IR department do not do general reading and are unrelated to the IR department, he sees the course as an opportunity to educate students. Yes, this can be a good feature, but I think most people do not read about the IR, so he often repeats it to make sure what he says is understood, or sometimes take the subject far back to lay the groundwork. It can be annoying for those who take the department seriously because it exceeds the duration of the lesson and the efficiency of the lesson decreases.

course: I think he should remove presentations from his classes. I think the reason he put a presentation in his class is because he wants to see those who do not come to the class doing a work and he wants us to practice for the group works that we will encounter in the future. As a result, presentations that are unorganized, expired, and that some make for the sake of making them appear. I would have preferred him to conduct the lecture in a seminar style rather than having us make a presentation. Not only does the lesson time pass with presentations (which I think most of us know we do not put forth a satisfactory work), but we also want to listen to him more, and I think the reason why students come to class is to listen to him.
